dataset.what_one_row_represents: One officially-named meteorite recognised by the Meteoritical Society's Nomenclature Committee (Fell = impact observed; Found = recovered later).
dataset.time_range: 860 CE - 2013 CE (with 1 typo at 2101 and 291 rows with no year)
dataset.geographic_scope: Global — 84% of rows are geocoded (16% missing lat/long); within geocoded rows, 59% are from Antarctica.

ana_01.label: Dataset profile
ana_01.content: The dataset contains 45,716 rows and 10 columns, with one row per officially-named meteorite. Of these, 1,107 (2.42%) are observed Fells and 44,609 (97.58%) are post-recovery Finds; 45,641 are Valid and only 75 are Relict (heavily weathered). The recclass column has 466 distinct values, the year column ranges from 860 to 2,101 (one typo) with 291 nulls, and mass(g) ranges from 0 to 60,000,000 with 131 nulls. Coordinates are missing for 7,315 rows (16.0%).

ana_04.label: Fell vs Found — 2.42% of all named meteorites were ever seen falling
ana_04.content: The headline split of the catalogue: 1,107 rows (2.42%) are Fells where a human witnessed the descent; 44,608 (97.58%) are Founds where the rock was recognised on the ground at some unknown later date. This is the single biggest selection effect in the dataset. The Detective's external benchmark — roughly 1,800 land-falls per year, of which only about 7–10 become observed-fall records — implies a true witnessing rate of well under 1%, consistent with what the dataset shows.

ana_05.label: Fells are 92x heavier than Founds at the median
ana_05.content: Fells and Founds have wildly different mass distributions. Median Fell mass is 2,800 g (about a 3-litre bottle of water); median Found mass is just 30.5 g (an espresso ladle). Geometric means tell the same story: 2,498 g for Fells vs 39 g for Founds — a 64x ratio. This is because the only meteorites loud and bright enough to be noticed mid-fall are the big ones, while Antarctic and desert searches pick up tiny fragments down to gram scale that would never trigger a witness.

ana_06.label: Decade-by-decade Fell vs Found counts (860-2010s)
ana_06.content: Decade-resolved counts trace the catalogue's growth. Before 1700 the record is almost entirely sparse Fells from Europe and East Asia (Nogata 860, Narni 920, Elbogen 1399, Ensisheim 1491). Fells grow modestly through the 1800s into a steady 50-90/decade in the 20th century. Founds stay below 100/decade until the 1960s, then explode: 4,909 in the 1970s, 6,766 in the 1980s, 11,563 in the 1990s, 17,698 in the 2000s. The 2010s entry (1,963) reflects the dataset being frozen ~2013.

ana_07.label: 96.8% of all Founds are post-1969 — Antarctica's signature
ana_07.content: Splitting the catalogue at 1970 (the cusp of systematic Antarctic recovery) shows that 42,886 of 44,317 dated Founds — 96.8% — were recognised in the last four-and-a-bit decades of the dataset. Fells barely budge: only 22.0% of dated Fells are post-1969 (244 out of 1,107). In other words, almost all of the Find growth is operational, not physical: rocks didn't suddenly start landing more often; humans suddenly started looking systematically.

ana_08.label: Mass distribution is log-normal over 10 orders of magnitude
ana_08.content: Meteorite masses span from sub-gram chips to the 60-tonne Hoba — ten orders of magnitude on a linear axis. The distribution is sharply log-normal: 36% of rows (16,373) sit in the 10-100 g bucket, with a long thin tail. Median mass is 32.7 g (about a tomato), mean is 13,284 g (about a cinder block) — the mean is 400x the median, the canonical signature of a heavy-tailed distribution. Geometric mean (43 g) is the meaningful 'typical' value. The 95th percentile is 4,000 g and the 99th is 50,600 g; only 52 rows (0.1%) exceed 1 tonne.

ana_10.label: Class families: ordinary chondrites are 87% of rows
ana_10.content: Collapsing the 466 distinct recclass strings into composition families gives a clean Pareto: Ordinary chondrites dominate at 86.96% (39,756 rows), followed by Carbonaceous chondrites at 3.50% (1,602), HED achondrites at 2.59% (1,186), Iron meteorites at just 2.34% (1,069), and a long tail of enstatite/primitive achondrites/stony-irons/lunar/Martian under 1.5% each. So irons — which dominate the heavy tail (ana_09) — are barely 1 in 43 rows by count. The Detective's '87% ordinary chondrite' benchmark from the literature lines up almost exactly with this dataset's 86.96%.

ana_14.label: Antarctica accounts for 59% of all geocoded Founds — and 0% of Fells
ana_14.content: Splitting at latitude -60° (the Antarctic Circle plus a buffer): 22,099 rows lie in Antarctica, every single one a Found, and zero Fells. Outside Antarctica, the catalogue is 1,097 Fells and 15,204 Founds — a much more balanced 6.73% Fell rate. So Antarctica alone supplies 59.2% of every geocoded Find in the dataset, and contributes nothing to the Fell record. No one is standing under Antarctic skies to watch a meteorite fall; the ice does the collecting passively, over millennia (det_04).

ana_15.label: Hot-desert recovery hotspots: Sahara, Arabia, US SW, Australia, Atacama
ana_15.content: Stripping out Antarctica and the rest-of-world residual, the dataset's other big concentrations are all desert recovery zones. ana_17.label: Oldest 10 entries — eight European Fells, two East-Asian (Nogata 860 CE the earliest)
ana_17.content: The oldest dated rows in the catalogue trace the very early history of meteorite witnessing. Nogata (860 CE, Japan, L6) is the oldest: an observed fall preserved as a Shinto temple relic in Fukuoka. Narni (920 CE, Italy) is next. Then five 15th-16th century European Fells — Elbogen (1399, Czech lands), Rivolta de Bassi (1490, Italy), Ensisheim (1491, France — the most famous medieval fall, still on display), Valdinoce (1495), Oliva-Gandia (1519, Spain). The first Find in the top 10 is Campo del Cielo, recorded 1575 — though its actual fall was ~4,500 years earlier (det_09).

ana_18.label: Modern Fell rate: ~6 observed falls per year worldwide
ana_18.content: Between 1900 and 2013 the catalogue records 707 observed Fells — a mean of 6.20 per year and a median of 6 per year. The peak was 17 Fells in 1933. This matches the Detective's external benchmark (7.9 reported falls/year averaged 2007-2018) almost exactly, and explains why Fells stay below 100/decade throughout the modern era while Founds explode (ana_06): the underlying physical witnessing rate is essentially flat, capped by how many humans are in the right place at the right time.

caveats.content: 16.0% of rows (7,315) have no coordinates. Any geographic analysis silently drops these — they likely include many old European Fells and historical entries with imprecise locations.
The dataset is frozen ~2013 (the 2010s decade has only 1,963 rows vs ~17,000 in the 2000s). Anything that says 'in the 2010s' or 'recently' is incomplete by design.

The recclass family classification is rules-based (regex on the recclass string) and approximate. Most 'Stone-uncl' entries from before 1860 were rolled into 'Other / Ungrouped'; this is why that bucket has an anomalous 30% Fell rate.
Mass values for very old meteorites are often the recovered mass, not the impact mass — the original meteoroid was almost certainly larger before atmospheric ablation and post-fall weathering.

The 5° x 5° hex grid in ana_16 distorts area near the poles (Antarctic cells cover far less ground than equatorial ones), inflating the apparent Antarctic concentration. The qualitative pattern is real, but the absolute cell counts are not directly comparable across latitudes.
